title: Teaching Students Why We Review Like We Do
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart credits a colleague, Jessica Lee, for a PD session on teaching students how to learn, which reframed his approach to pre-assessment review days. The core idea is that retrieval practice (testing yourself to pull information from memory) and interleaved practice (mixing older and newer material) work best when students are also told, in thirty seconds or less, why the activity is worth their time. He then narrates how he applied the idea before a unit assessment, running students through three back-to-back retrieval activities - a date-recall drill, a rapid-fire quiz, and a Jeopardy-style game - before asking students to reflect on how review could be improved next time. The piece is a concrete classroom translation of retrieval-practice research into a repeatable review-day format, with an explicit reminder that explaining the "why" behind the activity is itself part of what makes it effective.
points: Distills a colleague's PD session into two named mechanisms - retrieval practice and interleaved practice - as the engine behind effective review days.
Insists that explaining to students, in thirty seconds, why a review activity is worth their time is a "critical piece," not an optional add-on.
Demonstrates a repeatable three-activity review structure (date recall, rapid quiz, Jeopardy-style game) built entirely around interleaved retrieval before a unit assessment.
Closes the loop by having students reflect on how review could be improved next time, turning the activity into an iterative classroom routine rather than a one-off.
quotes: In my experience, we teachers can be deleteriously presumptuous about the degree to which our students understand how best to learn.
When students don't know how to learn, it can often be quite harmful to the level of effort they put forth in class. And we can hardly blame them for this

Retrieval practice: testing yourself on knowledge - that is, literally requiring yourself to pull information from memory and use it - is the best way to both know that you know it and ensure that you know.
Interleaved practice: mixing practice up to include skills and knowledge acquired both recently and further in the past.
when you conduct activities like this in your classroom, take thirty seconds to explain to students why this kind of activity is worth their time. That's a critical piece.
just be mindful with memorization like this that the quality with which the information is stored is the quality with which it tends to get retrieved
